**Start with surprise, not the formula.** Suppose a weather source says tomorrow has a 90% chance of sunshine. Sunshine would not surprise you much; rain would. Information theory measures the surprise of an outcome assigned probability $p$ by $-\log p$. A certain outcome has surprise zero because $-\log1=0$. An unlikely outcome has larger surprise. With base-two logarithms, surprise is measured in bits. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

Why a logarithm? For independent outcomes, probabilities multiply, but the information gained from observing both should add. The identity $-\log(p_1p_2)=-\log p_1-\log p_2$ gives precisely that behavior. This supplies intuition for the building block used by entropy and cross-entropy.

Let $P$ describe how outcomes actually occur, and let $Q$ describe the probabilities predicted by a model. For example, $P=(0.75,0.25)$ could be the true probabilities of sunshine and rain, while $Q=(0.5,0.5)$ is a model that predicts them equally often. Both distributions refer to the same outcomes and each sums to one.

![Original worked example: cross-entropy separates into fixed entropy and model mismatch.](/answer-diagrams/entropy-kl.svg)

**Entropy: the uncertainty in the source itself.** Entropy is average surprise when outcomes follow $P$ and are also scored using $P$:

$$H(P)=\mathbb E_{x\sim P}[-\log P(x)]=-\sum_xP(x)\log P(x).$$

Read the sum as “surprise of each outcome, weighted by how often it really happens.” A fair coin has entropy one bit: either result has surprise $-\log_2(0.5)=1$. A coin that always lands heads has entropy zero because there is nothing uncertain to learn. For our 75/25 weather example,

$$H(P)=-0.75\log_2(0.75)-0.25\log_2(0.25)\approx0.8113\text{ bits}.$$

Entropy is not a model error. Even a perfect model predicting 75/25 cannot know which particular outcome will occur; this remaining uncertainty belongs to the source. The coding interpretation is an ideal expected description length, with the usual asymptotic/coding qualifications rather than a claim that every single observation literally uses a fractional number of physical bits. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

**Cross-entropy: how surprised your model is by real observations.** Keep drawing outcomes from the real source $P$, but now calculate surprise using the model's prediction $Q$:

$$H(P,Q)=\mathbb E_{x\sim P}[-\log Q(x)]=-\sum_xP(x)\log Q(x).$$

The weighting still uses $P$ because reality determines which outcomes you see. The logarithm uses $Q$ because the model determines the probability assigned to each observation. Mixing up those roles changes the question being measured. This expected negative log-probability is the population version of the log loss used to train probabilistic classifiers. [2](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/) [4](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html)

For $P=(0.75,0.25)$ and $Q=(0.5,0.5)$, both model surprises equal one bit, so cross-entropy is exactly one bit. Now consider the confidently wrong $Q=(0.1,0.9)$: sunshine, which occurs frequently, receives only 10% model probability. Its cross-entropy is about 2.5294 bits. The large loss reflects repeated surprise about a common event—not merely whether the model's most likely class was right or wrong.

**KL divergence: the extra cost of using the wrong distribution.** Forward KL is

$$D_{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum_xP(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}.$$

The ratio compares true and model probabilities for each outcome; the average is taken under $P$. KL is nonnegative when defined, and zero when the distributions agree. It is not a distance metric: generally $D_{KL}(P\|Q)\ne D_{KL}(Q\|P)$, and it does not satisfy all metric properties. Individual terms may be negative; nonnegativity is a property of their full sum. [3](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book2.html)

For the 75/25 source and the 50/50 model, KL is $1-0.8113=0.1887$ bits. Think of this as extra average surprise caused by model mismatch. If the model becomes $Q=P$, cross-entropy falls to 0.8113 bits and KL falls to zero. The model has removed its avoidable mismatch, not the weather's inherent uncertainty.

**Derive the identity one step at a time.** Start with KL and split the logarithm of a ratio:

$$D_{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum_xP(x)[\log P(x)-\log Q(x)].$$

Distribute the sum:

$$D_{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum_xP(x)\log P(x)-\sum_xP(x)\log Q(x).$$

The first term is $-H(P)$; the second is $H(P,Q)$. Therefore,

$$H(P,Q)=H(P)+D_{KL}(P\|Q).$$

This is an exact algebraic identity, not an approximation or a special property of neural networks. It separates unavoidable source uncertainty from mismatch introduced by choosing $Q$.

**Why the two optimization problems are identical.** Write the model as $Q_\theta$, where $\theta$ contains its adjustable parameters. During training, assume the target distribution $P$ is fixed. Then

$$\underset{\theta}{\arg\min}\ H(P,Q_\theta)=\underset{\theta}{\arg\min}\ [H(P)+D_{KL}(P\|Q_\theta)]=\underset{\theta}{\arg\min}\ D_{KL}(P\|Q_\theta).$$

Adding the same constant to every candidate cannot change which candidate is best. If model A has lower KL than model B, it has lower cross-entropy by exactly the same difference. Where differentiation is valid, the gradients also agree because $\nabla_\theta H(P)=0$. This equivalence does not require the model family to contain the true distribution: even if perfect fitting is impossible, both objectives choose the same best available approximations. It does not promise that gradient descent finds a global optimum.

**Connect this to classification.** For an input with observed label $y$, a one-hot target assigns probability one to that class. Its cross-entropy reduces to $-\log Q_\theta(y|x)$: all other target weights are zero. Across many independent observations, averaging this loss estimates expected conditional cross-entropy. A single one-hot target has zero entropy, but that does not imply the real conditional label distribution is deterministic; repeated similar inputs may legitimately have different labels.

**Boundary cases worth understanding.** Use $0\log0=0$ by continuity. If $P(x)>0$ but $Q(x)=0$, the model declares a possible event impossible, producing infinite cross-entropy and KL. Natural logs produce nats instead of bits; changing the log base rescales both objectives by a positive constant and does not change their minimizers. Finally, the “constant entropy” argument assumes $P$ does not also change with $\theta$; if both distributions are trainable, that step must be revisited.
